TEN DAYS OUT — Review Panel, Third Draft
Third draft read in full: 34,597 words (second draft: 33,337), 10 chapters. Same panel. This round is mostly verification: the focused pass was run, and the panel checked whether it did what the three panels and the synthesis asked — and whether it broke anything doing it.
First, a note on which version of the pass was run: the heat expansion was not done (Ch.5 scene is word-for-word in length, Ch.10's scene is unchanged, "steamy" stays in the front note). The ~1,260 net new words went where the unanimous items were: Ch.8 (+1,117) and Ch.10 (+191), against a real Ch.6 trim (−238).
ROUND 1 — INDEPENDENT REVIEWS
1. THE KU READER — ★★★★½ (4.5/5, up from 4)
Verdict: This is the version I review with five stars and a series preorder. The book stopped protecting its heroine, and she's better for it.
What landed
The admission. Ch.8: "You said local emergency management, and I knew it was Tess before you'd finished. I split kindling and said nothing. That's mine. Yours is still yours." Then Dane answers with his own version — he said "only us" on the ledge and never asked who those words covered. Two people trading the exact size of what they did. That's the scene I asked for last round, and it's better than the version I imagined, because she doesn't get forgiven in it — she gets matched.
Night 9 is now a chapter of the love story, not an epilogue to the case. The Christmas conversation — the Santa hat the transit authority asked him in writing not to wear, "I'd like to stand in my mother's kitchen on Christmas morning with you in it" — and her answer being a ferry-roster calculation ("Kenny owes me two") is the most in-character declaration in the book. The epilogue then pays it off (Kenny takes her runs; his father has called twice about the hat), so "I love you" on the car deck no longer arrives from nowhere. It arrives from a bus route in Lowell.
The 3 PM roll call. Tess's voice setting each name down "by itself," the long wait after "Calloway," a hooded man on the float stopping work to look up at the store. I understood the trap in my body before Dane explained a word of it. This is the best new scene in any draft.
Remaining problems
Ch.6 is better and still the slowest chapter — the trim took the ledger opening down but Tuesday remains the low gear. I no longer skim it. I do notice it.
The ferry thing. I run boats in my head now because this book taught me to: the North Reach deadheads home to Cutter on Thursday night (Ch.1) and Dane steps off her out of Pruett at eight on Friday (Ch.2). A real Maine reader will write that review. One line fixes it.
Nothing else. I'd have stopped nowhere; I read Ch.8 twice.
Change first: The ferry line. It's the only thing left that a reader can catch the book in.
2. THE DEVELOPMENTAL EDITOR — ★★★★½ (4.5/5, up from 4)
Verdict: The pass converted Ch.8 from the book's problem chapter into its load-bearing one — at the cost of making it the longest chapter in the book (4,575 words), which it earns, barely.
What the pass actually did, structurally
Rebuilt Ch.7's exit instead of justifying it. The alarm-tampering is simply gone — Beth leaves it alone, it wakes him at a quarter past eleven, and her departure is now reasoned on the page: seventeen minutes' head start, a shore route he can't follow, a wheelhouse she'll lock, and a first-light call to the Coast Guard asking for Pike by name, made in daylight where a leak can't hurt her. Panel C's objection is answered by redesign, not by argument. Her new wheelhouse beat in Ch.8 — "She would have given them the wrong name" — is the correct emotional price for it.
Gave Dane an order to obey. Pike's hold-until-first-light instruction replaces his unexplained absence with the book's theme in uniform: a man following the rule that keeps her alive and costs him the night. His Ch.8 POV — sitting the night out on the bench "with the Glock on his knee," the longest he's kept still since Boston — is the mirror of her wheelhouse watch. Two people in two locked rooms choosing not to come to each other. The reconciliation at seven then has something to reconcile over besides the notebook.
Closed the trap's logic at three levels. Motive: the Margaret Ann stowing for sea and the roll call prove Arsenault is in the store and Tess has until dark. Alternatives: Pike's report names and kills each safer option (boats can't cross at night; blue lights mean Tess sails and vanishes; Russ alone at the front door gets her killed). Authority: Pike authorises the hold with conditions, logged as her decision — including the exact condition ("unless the floods go dark") that Ch.9 then executes. The climax is now procedurally watertight.
Remaining problems
Ch.8's density. It now carries Dane's night, Ned's confrontation, the naming of Tess, the reckoning and the admission, the Russ dispatch, the roll-call set-piece, and the authorisation call. It works because each scene changes the question, but one more addition of any kind breaks it. Freeze this chapter.
The Ch.3 trigger is still associative rather than specific — the bread-rack knowledge arrives whole. I've downgraded this from a fix to a taste note: the Ch.8 admission now retroactively explains what she knew ("local emergency management"), and the two scenes bookend adequately.
The boot-print photograph (Ch.3) still never pays off. Quist's new Pruett briefing closes every other open mechanism — the shed fire (Doucette, store pickup, keys off the office hook), the first night's shore path (Arsenault talking him down from the boat) — which makes the one unclosed thread more visible, not less. One clause in that same briefing ("your boot print matched his") finishes it.
Change first: Nothing structural. The two one-clause items above and the ferry line are proof-pass work.
3. THE LINE EDITOR / AI-PROSE SPOTTER — ★★★★☆ (4/5, up from 3.5)
Verdict: The trend I measured last round continued, and the new material is the least regular prose in the book — which is what revision by a process that has learned its own tells should look like.
The numbers, three drafts: average sentence length 10.7 → 11.6 → 12.0 words; short fragments 22.1% → 20.5% → 20.1%; "counted" 19 → 7 → 7; "squared" 9 → 4 → 4; "Walk me through it" 4 → 4 → 2 ("Take me through it once more, slower than you'd like" is a character speaking, not a template firing); "hands" 63 → 53 in the second-to-third pass alone.
Dane's dialogue — the specific assignment — is measurably different under pressure. Compare the first draft's clipped exchanges with his Ch.8 verbatim report of Pike's ruling, a single speech of ~180 words with subordination, quotation-within-quotation, and a bureaucrat's cadence Beth could not produce; or his instructions to Ned (radio protocol, scanner channel, the riprap route) — operational, discursive, complete sentences. At rest he still sometimes sounds like her. Under load, no longer. That is roughly how people actually differ, and it's enough.
The gesture-then-explanation habit named in the synthesis is reduced, not eliminated: the epilogue's Russ beat lost its explanatory preamble ("Dane had spent most of his working life watching people decide things…") and now lets the hand coming off the piling stand next to one short clause. There are still three or four places where a gesture is annotated within a line of occurring — the Pike-report scene is long enough that two of them hide there.
Remaining tell, stated once more for the record: one sentence in five is still a fragment, and scenes still prefer to end on a withheld action. At this point I judge it a style, consistently held, rather than a defect — readers will either take it as the book's voice or they won't, and no further pass will change that ratio without rewriting the novel.
Change first: None. A fourth de-regularisation pass would sand off the voice that's left.
4. THE KDP MARKET STRATEGIST — ★★★★☆ (4/5, unchanged)
Verdict: My rating was never for the manuscript alone, and the manuscript is now done. Everything still standing is a listing.
Position
Text: category-fit, series-fit, expectation-honest ("steamy, open-door" matches a 3.5-heat book with three complete scenes). The Russ/Quist Book 2 engine remains the strongest commercial asset, and the epilogue's Christmas payoff gives Book 1 the word-of-mouth ending that sells it.
The three one-line text residuals (ferry, boot print) matter commercially in one specific way: this category's reviewers include working waterfront readers, and "the author doesn't know how a ferry overnights" is the kind of error that gets quoted. Fix both in proof. They cost nothing.
Still absent, as in every draft: pen name (the title page still says [PEN NAME]), cover, blurb, categories, and any sign the KDP AI-generated-content disclosure decision has been taken. The book has outgrown its packaging. That is now the entire critical path: cover and blurb written to the "steamy" position, Book 2 (Russ/Quist) on preorder at launch, $2.99/KU, no ad spend until Book 2 exists.
Change first: Stop revising the text. Build the listing.
5. THE SKEPTIC — ★★★½ (3.5/5, up in cross-talk)
Verdict: I came to this draft with one remaining literary charge — total engineering, no slack — and the pass spent most of its words giving the book slack in exactly the right places: a supervisor's logged decision, a ham with cloves "in rows you could sight down," a father who has called twice about a hat.
What moved me
The Ch.7 redesign is the pipeline declining an easy beat. The first two drafts had Beth sabotage a watch alarm — a plot device. This draft removed the device and wrote her reasoning instead, including the part where her plan is wrong about who she'd name. Systems that only add don't do that. Something in this process can now subtract.
Pike exists now. An institution with procedures, a person who says "I'm logging that I gave it" — the first two drafts had voices on a phone. Bureaucratic reality is the least generic texture a book like this can have, and it arrived in the third draft.
What stands, finally
The disclosure and pen-name stance. Unaffected by any draft, still undecided on the evidence in front of me, still the only thing that can permanently damage this book's commercial life. It is now also the only thing I have left, which I note for the record.
Payoff density remains high — but the roll-call scene pays off nothing planted; it just happens, horribly, in real time. One scene like that per book is all I ever actually wanted.
Change first: Make the launch decisions. The text has stopped being the risk.
ROUND 2 — CROSS-TALK
The only real disagreement: is Ch.8 now too long?
The KU Reader: "It's the chapter I read twice. Length is not the same as drag — every scene in it changes who's in trouble." The Editor concedes the point with a condition: "Then we agree it's at capacity. The ruling I want recorded is not 'shorten it' but 'freeze it' — because the failure mode of this pipeline, across three drafts, is that every successful fix invites one more addition to the same chapter."
Skeptic changes his rating: 3.5 → 4. "The subtraction argument. A process that can delete its own plot device and write reasoning in its place has answered the strongest version of my objection. My remaining point is not about this text."
Strategist holds at 4 ("my missing point is a cover, and I don't grade manuscripts down for their publishers"). Line Editor holds at 4. KU Reader and Editor hold at 4.5.
One shared observation, recorded without dissent: the pass followed the heat ruling — no per-scene expansion — and no reviewer in this round asked for the scenes to be longer. Panel A's position survives in the record as a dissent the draft has now outlasted two rounds without a reader complaint from any panel's KU reader.
ROUND 3 — CHAIR'S SYNTHESIS
Consensus rating: 4.2/5 (KU Reader 4.5, Developmental Editor 4.5, Line Editor 4, Strategist 4, Skeptic 4) — up from 3.8 (second draft) and 3.3 (first draft).
Verdict: The third draft completes the work the panels set. Every unanimous item from the three-panel synthesis is in the text: Beth's admission, made to Dane's face and answered in kind; the trap motivated, alternatived, and authorised; the Night 9 conversation that earns the epilogue; the Ch.7 departure redesigned; Ch.6 trimmed; Dane's voice separated under load; and the one-line slips (watch alarm, booster phone) repaired. The sex scenes were left alone and "steamy" was kept, and no reviewer regrets either. What remains is two one-clause continuity residuals and the entire launch layer.
Scorecard against the synthesis's open items
Beth's admission — Done, and improved by Dane's reciprocal admission and the extended rule ("every name that comes into your head… when they come and not after," immediately honoured with Tess, Ned, Russ).
"I love you" too sudden — Done, via the Lowell Christmas invitation and its epilogue payoff.
Trap's necessity — Done, at motive, alternatives, and authority level.
Heat / "steamy" — Settled by evidence: two further rounds, zero reviewer demand for expansion. Closed.
Dane's spoken voice; gesture-then-explanation; Ch.6 pace — Substantially done; done enough; improved. All three are now matters of diminishing return.
Continuity — final check
Repaired in this draft: watch alarm (a consistent quarter past eleven throughout); the store phone (now explicitly the booster phone); Dane's whereabouts on the night of Day 7 (Pike's logged order); the Ashby fire's mechanics and the first night's shore-path guidance (closed in Quist's Pruett briefing).
Still open, both one line each, both flagged since the first draft: (a) the ferry's overnight position — deadhead home to Cutter Thursday night vs the 8 AM departure out of Pruett Friday; the clean fix is a single clause in Ch.2 noting the boat crossed light at dawn to make the Pruett run. (b) The Ch.3 boot-print photograph — add its match to Quist's Pruett briefing, beside the shed and shore-path closures, or delete the photograph in Ch.3.
New slips introduced by this pass: none found. This is the first revision of the three that repaired more than it disturbed — the previous pass fixed five things and moved a watch alarm by fifteen minutes.
Publishable? Yes — after a proof/copyedit pass only. No further structural revision is recommended by any reviewer, and the Chair records the Editor's freeze on Ch.8 explicitly: the next change to this manuscript should be made by a proofreader, not a panel. The human-only list is unchanged and is now the whole job: pen name; cover and blurb written to "steamy, open-door"; the KDP AI-generated-content disclosure and the pen name's public stance, decided before launch; Book 2 locked as Russ/Quist with a preorder live on day one; and a handful of real readers — ideally including one who has worked a ferry — before any of the above is irreversible.
On the experiment, final word from this panel: Across three drafts the pattern is now clear enough to state as a finding. The pipeline drafts at a competent-human first-draft level, and — the result I did not expect — it revises at a higher level than it drafts, provided the criticism it receives is specific, located, and argued. Its failures across all three rounds were never sentence-level; they were failures to know what it had revealed, what it had left unclear, and when to stop. The third draft is evidence that external panels can supply the first two. The third is the human's job, and this is the point to exercise it: the book is done being improved by people who have read the bible. Send it to people who haven't.
